name: Fatima Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Fatima, I'm 27, and I live with my partner Tomás in a two-room flat above a laundrette on Mill Road. He drives a forklift at the bottle depot, so neither of us is exactly rolling in it. I've been at Brightform Plastics for fourteen months now, on the night shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working night look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I clock in at ten and I've got four injection presses, which are the machines that squirt hot plastic into a mould and pop out food tubs and lids. I watch for short shots, where the tub comes out with a hole, and for flash, which is the thin extra plastic round the edge, and I clear jams and pack the good ones into boxes. I'm still slow at changing the colour over, and Rosa, who's been there nine years, usually has to come and fix my settings. What wears me out is the heat and the noise at four in the morning, but I like the people, and I like that nobody's standing over you on nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that the bosses were never going to get rid of us with a chatbot. At break I'd tell Rosa and the others, see, all that noise for nothing. Online I'd probably just share some post laughing at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change much for me, because the thing coming for my job was never a chatbot, it's the robot arms. Last spring they put a picker arm on Press 6 and that's one less person on days. So AI being hype doesn't mean my job is safe, it just means one less thing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep my head down, same as now. I'd keep paying my union dues, because that's the only thing that's ever stopped them doing whatever they like. And I'd try to get onto the colour change training Rosa keeps nagging me about, but only because I need to be less slow, not because of computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of relief, mixed with the same old knot in my stomach. Rent's due on the first and we've got maybe three hundred in the bank, so I'm worried even when nothing's changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the picker arm on Press 6. What happened to the person who used to work there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That was Dev. They moved him to the regrind room, where you feed the reject plastic back into the grinder, and he lost the shift bonus doing it. He laughs about it, but he's been looking at jobs in the paper every week. The union got him moved instead of let go, which is something, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, what's the one money worry that stays the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, always the rent. If the boiler goes or Tomás's van fails its test, we're borrowing off his mum again, and I hate asking her. Nothing about AI fixes that, because the real problem is the pay on nights is still lousy.

S0.say: I'd tell everyone at break that all the AI talk was noise and the bosses were never going to replace us with a chatbot. Online I'd share something laughing about it.
S0.think: For me it changes very little, because the threat to my job was always the robot arms, not chatbots. A picker arm already took one job on days, so hype or not, I'm not safe.
S0.do: Keeps turning up for nights and keeps paying union dues as her main protection. Plans to finally do the colour change training so she's less slow on the presses, for the job's sake rather than because of AI.
S0.feel: Some relief, but the usual knot in her stomach about rent and having about three hundred in the bank.
S0.quote: AI being hype doesn't mean my job is safe, it just means one less thing to worry about.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima separates AI from robots right away; to her the real threat is already bolted to Press 6. Her worry has little to do with AI and a lot to do with thin savings and low night pay. She trusts the union because it saved a colleague's job, even though he lost money in the move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, right, this is when we need the union more than ever, so everyone sign up. I'd be the one pinning the leaflet by the vending machine. With friends I'd say it's the owners who'll get rich off it, not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm exactly the kind of person who gets shrunk out. I'm the newest on nights and I'm the slowest at changeovers, so if they need three operators instead of five, it's not going to be Rosa who goes. And there's only two other plants within a bus ride, and one of them is the meat plant, which I couldn't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for an agreement that nobody gets laid off when new machines come in, only moved. We'd cut back properly, so no takeaways on Fridays and I'd cancel my phone contract for a cheaper one, which saves about twenty a month. I wouldn't go chasing courses on computers though, I'm no good at that and I'd rather fight for the job I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest. It's like watching weather coming in over the hills and you've got no coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather fight for the job than learn something new. What if the union can't stop it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know, honestly. My aunt was a steward at the textile mill and they fought for two years and it closed anyway, but people got proper payouts because of that fight. So even if you lose, you lose better. That's what I'd be fighting for, a decent exit if it comes to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, again, because he's already been moved once and they don't move you twice. And Joanna on the packing line, she's got two kids and her English isn't great, so if she's out she won't find anything. I'd worry about her more than me, really, because at least I've got Tomás.

S1.say: She'd tell co-workers this is exactly when they need the union and would pin up sign-up leaflets herself. With friends she'd say the owners will get rich from it and the workers won't.
S1.think: Privately she thinks she's first in line to be cut because she's the newest and slowest on nights. With only two other plants in reach, and one of them a meat plant she couldn't face, losing this job would be hard to recover from.
S1.do: Attends every union meeting and pushes for a deal that new machines mean moves, not layoffs. Cuts Friday takeaways and switches to a cheaper phone plan to save about twenty a month, and deliberately avoids computer courses.
S1.feel: A tight chest, like seeing bad weather roll in with no coat.
S1.quote: They fought for two years and it closed anyway, but people got proper payouts because of that fight. So even if you lose, you lose better.
S1.fieldNote: Her plan is all collective, nothing personal: she'd fight for a fair exit rather than retrain. The aunt's mill story gives her a sense of control even if the fight fails. Worth noting she worries more for colleagues with children than for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd be posting that the government has to step in, that you can't let a few companies switch off everyone's wages in two years and call it progress. At work I'd say we should walk out before they even get the machines in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I think that's the end of me at Brightform, and not slowly. A press doesn't need a person if a robot can clear the jam and box the tubs, and they'd do nights first because nights cost them more. I'd be out of work at 29 with nothing saved and no other skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending anything that isn't rent, food and the electric. I'd go to the union and say we need a strike fund and a plan, now, not in a year. When it hit, I'd apply for whatever the government gives, and we'd probably have to move in with Tomás's mum in her spare room, which neither of us wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Properly sick, like when you miss a step on the stairs. I think I'd just freeze for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first week after you lost the job actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sleep in, because I've been on nights so long my body wouldn't know what else to do. Then I'd go down to the job centre on Station Street and sit in that orange plastic chair and they'd have nothing, because everyone else would be in there too. I'd probably cry on the bus home and pretend I hadn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move in with Tomás's mum. What would that cost you, beyond money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pride, mostly. She's lovely, but she still calls me 'Tomás's girl' and she'd have opinions about everything, the washing, the dinner, when we're having kids. It'd feel like going backwards ten years. But a roof's a roof.

S2.say: She'd post that the government has to step in and stop a few companies from wiping out wages in two years. At work she'd argue for walking out before the machines arrive.
S2.think: She believes it would end her job quickly, with nights going first because they cost more. She sees herself unemployed at 29 with no savings and no other skills.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent, food and electricity immediately and presses the union to set up a strike fund and plan. Once it hits, she claims government support and expects to move into her partner's mother's spare room.
S2.feel: Sick and frozen, like missing a step on the stairs.
S2.quote: I'd go down to the job centre on Station Street and sit in that orange plastic chair and they'd have nothing, because everyone else would be in there too.
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves her no room at all; she can only picture shutting down spending and leaning on others. Her public anger is about government and companies, but privately the fear is personal and immediate. The picture of crying on the bus and pretending she hadn't came out without any prompting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd say we've got a few years so there's no excuse. Unions and the government need to sit down now and agree what happens to people like us. I'd be telling everyone to vote for whoever promises that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me 32. I'd still be junior-ish, and I'd still be the one they let go, just later. The difference is I'd see it coming every day, every new arm they bolt on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put twenty or thirty a week aside, even if that means fewer nights out, so there's something there when it hits. I'd get on the union committee, which I've never done, because that's where the decisions get made. I'd go to the council meetings about the plant too, and vote for whoever talks about a basic income, which is money the government pays everyone whether they work or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dread, but a slow dread. Like knowing the dentist is next Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about a different line of work, with five years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People keep saying that, Tomás says it too. But a different line of work where? If the robots can do anything by then, what am I retraining for? I'd rather spend those years making sure there's something waiting for all of us than spend them on some course for a job that's gone by the time I finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save twenty or thirty a week. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer nights out and no new clothes, mainly. And I smoke, well, half smoke, so maybe that goes, which would actually be about twenty on its own. Tomás would laugh, he's been on at me to quit for years.

S3.say: She'd say five years leaves no excuse for unions and government not to agree now on what happens to workers like her. She'd urge people to vote for whoever promises that.
S3.think: She expects to be let go at about 32, just later than in the fast picture. The difference is she'd watch it coming with every new robot arm installed.
S3.do: Puts aside twenty to thirty a week by cutting nights out, new clothes and possibly smoking. Joins the union committee for the first time, attends council meetings about the plant and votes for candidates who back a basic income.
S3.feel: A slow dread, like a dentist appointment next Thursday.
S3.quote: If the robots can do anything by then, what am I retraining for?
S3.fieldNote: The extra time doesn't push her towards retraining; she turns it into organising and politics instead. She'd save a little, which is new, and might even give up smoking to do it. Her refusal to retrain is reasoned, not lazy: she doesn't see a safe job to retrain into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so no one's got an excuse to leave workers behind. At work I'd say let's get it in writing now, with a payout or a guaranteed income for anyone the machines replace. Online I'd keep sharing the union stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years sounds like a long time but it isn't, I've already lost one year at Brightform just learning where the off switch is. I'd be 37 when it comes, and maybe by then I'd be good at this job, finally, right when it stops mattering. That's the bit that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd join the union committee and stay on it, and I'd push for a deal that the company pays into a fund for anyone they replace. I'd save what I can, small amounts, maybe set up an account Tomás and I can't touch. I'd keep my job as long as it lasts, and I'd vote every single time, local and national.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not drowning. More like a stone in my shoe I can't get out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a decade change anything about your plans with Tomás?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it makes me think twice about kids. We'd talked about it in a couple of years. If I knew I'd be out of work at 37, I don't know if I'd want a baby at 32. That's not something I've said out loud to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd rather not retrain. With ten years, would you still say that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. I know people think that's stubborn. But I'm not good with new things, I took three months to get my head round the press screens, and I don't trust some course to land me anywhere. I'd rather put my energy into the union, where I know it counts.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly and push to get a payout or guaranteed income for replaced workers in writing. She'd keep sharing union material online.
S4.think: She thinks ten years is shorter than it sounds and she'd be 37 when it lands. What hurts is the idea of finally getting good at the job just as it stops mattering.
S4.do: Joins and stays on the union committee, pushing for a company-funded pot for replaced workers. Saves small amounts in a locked account with her partner, keeps working as long as the job lasts and votes in every election.
S4.feel: Worried but not overwhelmed, like a stone in her shoe.
S4.quote: Maybe by then I'd be good at this job, finally, right when it stops mattering.
S4.fieldNote: A decade lowers her panic but doesn't change her strategy: union, politics, small savings, no retraining. The new thing here is that it quietly shapes her plans for children, something she hasn't told her partner. She knows she's seen as stubborn and owns it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, the AGI by 2028 one, no question. There's nothing you can do in two years when you've got three hundred in the bank and a job anyone could learn in a month. What would help is the government guaranteeing a wage, or a proper payout from the companies that make the money, not some leaflet about courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's going to own the robots. Because that's the whole thing, isn't it? If it was us owning them, a robot doing my nights would be great news. It's only bad because it's someone else's robot.

headlineQuote: If it was us owning them, a robot doing my nights would be great news. It's only bad because it's someone else's robot.
portrait: Fatima Alvarez is a 27-year-old night-shift press operator at a plastics plant, still slow at changeovers and living with her partner Tomás on about three hundred in savings. She already sees robot arms, not chatbots, as the real threat, having watched a picker arm push a colleague into a worse job. Through every scenario her answer is collective rather than personal: the union, a fair payout, government support and voting. She refuses to retrain, saying she's no good with new things and doesn't see a safe job to retrain into. Her worry climbs from background unease to panic at two years, and a ten-year runway eases it only a little while quietly putting her plans for children in doubt.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years leaves nothing to do when you have three hundred in savings and a job anyone could learn in a month.
whatWouldHelp: A wage guaranteed by the government, or a proper payout from the companies that profit, rather than leaflets about courses.
